13590:
A remittance is money that someone sends to another person — usually across a long distance, and most often across international borders.

Think of it this way: the word captures the idea of sending money away from where you are, to someone who is somewhere else. The money you send is the remittance.
The Most Common Use: Money Sent Home by Migrants

This is where you will encounter the word most often.

Imagine a man from a small town in Bihar who goes to work in Dubai. Every month, he earns a salary. He keeps some for his own expenses in Dubai, but he sends a portion back to his wife and parents in Bihar. That money he sends home — that is a remittance.

This kind of remittance is called a personal remittance or an international remittance. It is money that flows from a worker living in one country to their family living in another country.

This happens on a massive scale around the world. Millions of people — from India, the Philippines, Mexico, Bangladesh, Nepal, and many other countries — work abroad and regularly send money home to support their families. These regular transfers of money are all remittances.

For example:

  • A nurse from Kerala working in the UK sends £500 to her parents every month → that £500 is a remittance.
  • A construction worker from Nepal working in Qatar sends money to his wife → that is a remittance.
  • An IT professional from India working in the US sends money to pay for his parents' medical bills back home → that is a remittance.
The Second Use: Payment Sent to Settle a Debt or Invoice

The word "remittance" is also used in business and finance to mean a payment sent to clear an outstanding bill, invoice, or debt.

Imagine a company buys raw materials from a supplier on credit. After 30 days, the company sends the payment to the supplier to settle what it owes. This payment can be called a remittance.

You will often see the phrase "remittance advice" in this context. A remittance advice is simply a document or note that the payer sends along with the payment to tell the recipient: "Here is the money I owe you, and this is which invoice or debt it is paying off." It is essentially a notification that accompanies a payment.

Notice that both uses share the same fundamental concept: money that is sent from one party to another. The difference is just in context:

ContextWhat "remittance" refers to
Migration / working abroadMoney sent by a worker to their family in another country
Business / financeA payment sent to settle a bill, invoice, or outstanding debt

In everyday conversation and news, when people say "remittance," they almost always mean the first sense — money sent home by migrant workers. In formal business documents, "remittance" is used more for the second sense.

Remittances are not handed over in person. Since the sender and receiver are physically far apart, the money travels through financial channels. Common methods include:

  • Bank wire transfers — the sender's bank directly transfers money to the receiver's bank account.
  • Money transfer services — companies like Western Union, MoneyGram, or Wise specialize in moving money across borders quickly.
  • Mobile apps — in recent years, apps and digital platforms have made it easier and cheaper to send remittances.
  • Informal channels — in some cases, money is sent through trusted individuals or unofficial networks, though this is less safe.

Each of these methods may charge a transfer fee and apply an exchange rate, which affects how much money the receiver actually gets.

For many families and even entire countries, remittances are a vital source of income.

  • For the receiving family, it might pay for food, rent, children's school fees, healthcare, or savings.
  • For the receiving country, remittances can represent a significant portion of the national economy. For instance, remittances to India and the Philippines run into hundreds of billions of dollars collectively each year, and for smaller countries like Nepal and Sri Lanka, remittances are one of the largest sources of foreign income.

This is why governments, economists, and international organizations pay close attention to remittance flows — they tell you a lot about how global migration and economies are connected.

It helps to see how "remittance" differs from words that sound related:

  • Payment: Any exchange of money for goods, services, or debts. Very broad. A remittance is a specific type of payment — one that is sent from a distance.
  • Transfer: The movement of money or assets from one account or person to another. Remittance is a type of transfer, but with a stronger implication of sending money from afar or to settle an obligation.
  • Wire transfer: This is the method of sending money electronically. A remittance is the money itself (or the act of sending it). You might send a remittance via a wire transfer.
  • Donation: Money given voluntarily without expectation of anything in return. A remittance is not a gift to a stranger — it is typically sent to fulfil a responsibility (supporting family) or to settle a debt.

Here are examples that show how the word is naturally used:

  • "India is one of the top recipients of global remittances, receiving money from its diaspora working across the Gulf, the US, and Europe."
  • "He has been sending a remittance of ₹20,000 every month to his parents since he moved to Singapore."
  • "Please find enclosed our remittance of $3,500 in settlement of invoice #4821."
  • "Remittance fees charged by banks can eat into the money that migrants send home."
  • "The government introduced policies to make it easier for the diaspora to send remittances back home."

A remittance is money that is sent from one person or organisation to another, across a distance — most commonly referring to money sent by a migrant worker to their family in their home country, but also used in business to mean a payment sent to clear a debt or invoice.

The word emphasises not just that money changed hands, but that it was dispatched — sent away from one place to reach someone in another.
13591:
A remnant is what is left behind after the main or largest part of something has gone, been used up, destroyed, or taken away. It is the surviving portion of something that was once bigger, fuller, or more complete.

Think of it this way: imagine a large candle. You burn it for many hours until almost nothing is left — just a small stub sitting in the holder. That stub is a remnant. It is small, it survived, and it represents what was once a whole, tall candle.

The crucial point is this: a remnant is not just any random piece of something. It is specifically the surviving piece of something that was once larger. The word gets its entire meaning from that contrast — something existed in its fullness, most of it is now gone, and this is what's left.
What Separates a "Remnant" from Just "a Piece"

If you cut a ribbon in half and use both halves equally, neither piece is a remnant. But if you use almost all of the ribbon and set aside just a short leftover bit, that bit is a remnant — because it's what survived after the main bulk was used up.

So whenever you use the word "remnant," you are quietly telling a three-part story: there was something whole and substantial before, most of it has since disappeared, and this small surviving portion is what remains. Remove any one of those three parts, and the word no longer fits.

The word works very naturally with tangible, physical things.

In fabric stores, remnants are the short leftover pieces of cloth that remain on a roll after most of the fabric has been cut and sold. They're smaller, often cheaper, and are simply what's left over after the main selling is done.

After a large dinner party, the remnants of the meal are the scraps and leftover bits of food still sitting on the table after everyone has eaten and gone home.

If you visit an ancient ruin, you might be walking through the remnants of a great temple — a few crumbling columns and broken stone walls, standing where a magnificent structure once existed in full.

After a wildfire tears through a forest, the ash, scorched trees, and burnt debris that remain are the remnants of the forest — what the fire left behind.

"Remnant" isn't limited to physical things. It works just as naturally with feelings, ideas, cultures, and situations.

If someone has endured a long, painful struggle but still feels the faintest flicker of optimism, you could say there are remnants of hope in them. Most of the hope has been worn down, but a trace of it is still alive.

If an ancient civilization has mostly vanished — its people gone, its language lost, its cities buried under centuries of earth — but a few artifacts and customs have survived, those are the remnants of that civilization. They are what made it through when nearly everything else was lost.

After a friendship ends, you might still share a habit you picked up from that person, a memory that surfaces now and then, or perhaps a mutual friend you still see. These are remnants of the friendship — small surviving traces of what was once a full, living bond.

"Remnant" can also describe a small surviving group of people, after a larger group has been scattered, destroyed, or drastically reduced in number.

"A small remnant of the community survived the disaster and slowly began to rebuild."

Here, the vast majority of the community is gone. The few who made it through — the remnant — carry on as the last representatives of something that was once much larger.

This is subtle but important, and it's what makes "remnant" a richer word than it might first appear. Almost always, it carries a quiet emotional undertone — a sense of loss (most of the original thing is gone), survival (this small piece made it through), and memory (it points back to what once was).

A remnant is not just a neutral piece of something. It is a witness to something that has mostly passed. When you call something a remnant, you are acknowledging that it belongs to a larger story — one where the main chapter has already closed, and this is all that remains of it.

Since you're learning, understanding how "remnant" sits among similar words will sharpen your grasp of it considerably.

Remains is broader and more neutral. It doesn't necessarily imply something once large or complete. A remnant specifically points to the contrast with a fuller original.

Vestige describes a trace so faint it has nearly vanished entirely — more extreme than a remnant. A vestige is barely perceptible; a remnant is small but still recognizable and meaningful.

Relic is something from the past that has been intentionally preserved, often for historical or sentimental reasons. A relic is kept on purpose; a remnant simply happened to survive.

Leftover is informal and everyday. Saying "leftovers from dinner" is casual kitchen talk. Saying "remnants of the meal" sounds more thoughtful, and is more naturally used in writing or meaningful speech.

Fragment implies something broken off, often suddenly. A fragment might come from a sharp break; a remnant tends to come from a gradual process of loss, use, or decay over time.
A Simple Way to Test If "Remnant" Fits

Whenever you're unsure whether to use this word, ask yourself three questions: Was there once a larger, more complete whole? Has most of it been lost, used up, or destroyed? Is what you're looking at the small surviving portion? If the answer to all three is yes, "remnant" is exactly the right word.
13592:
A remonstrance is a serious, earnest protest or objection that someone openly expresses — usually with reasons — aimed at stopping, changing, or drawing attention to something they believe is wrong, unfair, or unwise.

It's not a quiet grumble under your breath. It's not casual dissatisfaction. A remonstrance is when someone steps forward and makes their objection known — clearly, firmly, and with purpose.

Think of it this way. Imagine your manager at work suddenly decides to cut everyone's lunch break in half without any explanation. You don't just silently accept it. You go to them and say, "This is unfair, here is why it's unfair, and I want you to reconsider." That act of formally voicing your strong disagreement — with reasons behind it — is a remonstrance.

Or imagine a group of parents who are deeply unhappy about a new school policy. They write a letter to the school board laying out exactly why they oppose the policy and urging the board to reverse it. That letter is a remonstrance.

A remonstrance has three ingredients:

1. A strong objection or protest. Not a mild preference, but a real, firm disagreement with something — an action, a decision, a behavior, or a situation.

2. Reasons given. A remonstrance isn't just "I don't like this." It typically comes with an explanation — why something is wrong, unfair, or problematic. This is what separates it from a tantrum or a vague complaint.

3. A target. A remonstrance is directed at someone — a person, an authority, an institution — whose behavior or decision you want to influence or change.
The Tone and Weight of the Word

Remonstrance carries a sense of gravity and seriousness. It implies that the person making it genuinely cares about the issue, has thought it through, and is speaking up with conviction rather than impulse. It's a dignified word — it suggests the protest is reasoned and earnest, not hysterical or petty.

It can describe a spoken exchange ("his remonstrance fell on deaf ears") or something written and formal ("the citizens submitted a remonstrance to the council"). It can happen between two individuals — a parent making a remonstrance to a careless child, a friend objecting to another friend's harmful choices — or it can be large in scale, like an organized group formally protesting to a government.

Importantly, the person making a remonstrance almost always hopes to bring about a change. They're not just venting. There is an intention behind it: persuade the other side to stop, reconsider, or do better.

It's stronger than a simple complaint, which can be passive and unfocused. It's also stronger than a suggestion, which is mild and optional. But it's not quite as aggressive or confrontational as a demand or a condemnation.

A remonstrance sits in the territory of a firm, reasoned, respectful-but-serious protest. You are not ordering someone. You are not attacking them. But you are making absolutely clear that you object, and you are pressing them to take notice.

Think of it on a scale:

Mild end → grumble... complaint... objection... remonstrance... demand... condemnation → Strong end

A remonstrance leans toward the stronger side without crossing into hostility or ultimatum.

One of the most famous real-world examples is the Grand Remonstrance of 1641 in England. The English Parliament drafted a long, detailed document addressed to King Charles I, listing hundreds of grievances — complaints about how he was governing the country — and demanding that he change his ways. That document was literally called a "remonstrance" because that is precisely what it was: a serious, formal, reasoned protest directed at authority, with the aim of changing behavior.

This example also shows you that the word can be used for something large and historic, not just everyday arguments.

Here are some examples that show the word in natural use:

  • Despite her repeated remonstrances, her brother refused to return the money he owed her.
  • The employees' remonstrance against the new policy was ignored by upper management.
  • He listened to her remonstrance patiently but showed no intention of changing his behavior.
  • The council received a remonstrance from local residents about the planned construction.

Notice that in each case, someone is strongly and deliberately objecting to something, usually making their case to someone who has the power to change it.

The verb form of this word is remonstrate — meaning to make a remonstrance. "She remonstrated with him" means she made her objection known to him, firmly and with reasons. Knowing the verb helps you understand the noun even better: a remonstrance is simply the act or instance of remonstrating.

A remonstrance is a firm, earnest, and reasoned protest or objection — voiced openly to someone whose actions or decisions you oppose, with the hope of making them stop, reconsider, or change course. It is more serious and purposeful than a casual complaint, but more measured and dignified than an outright attack. Whenever someone stands up and says, in effect, "I strongly object to this, and here is why you should change it," — that is a remonstrance.
13593:
To remonstrate means to protest or object to something firmly and earnestly — and crucially, to do so by presenting reasons. It is not just expressing displeasure. It is making your case. You are not simply saying "I don't like this." You are saying "Here is why this is wrong, unfair, or misguided — and you should reconsider."

Think of it as a blend of protesting and reasoning at the same time.

Remonstrating sits in a very specific emotional and social space. It is:

More than complaining — Complaining can be passive; you might complain to a friend about your boss. But when you remonstrate, you go directly to the person responsible and raise your objection to their face, with reasons.

Less than quarrelling — Remonstrating is not a heated fight or an angry outburst. It carries a sense of seriousness and dignity. The person remonstrating is controlled, not raging.

Earnest and purposeful — The person remonstrating genuinely wants to change something — a decision, a behavior, a course of action. There is intent behind it, not just venting.

So the word lives somewhere between a calm but firm objection and a strong, reasoned protest. It implies that the speaker feels something is wrong enough to speak up about it directly, but is doing so with composure and argument rather than anger.
How It Is Used in a Sentence

This verb almost always comes with two small but important words attached to it:

  • You remonstrate with someone — meaning the person you are addressing.
  • You remonstrate about or over something — meaning the issue at hand.

Examples:

  • She remonstrated with her manager about the sudden change in her work schedule.

(She went to her manager and argued firmly that the change was unfair or wrong.)

  • The parents remonstrated with the school over its new disciplinary policy.

(The parents raised reasoned objections directly to the school.)

  • He remonstrated with his friend about the reckless decision.

(He urged his friend, with clear reasoning, to reconsider.)

You can also use it followed by "that" to include what exactly was said:

  • She remonstrated that the punishment was far too harsh for such a minor mistake.

And sometimes it is used without specifying who or what — especially in narration:

  • He tried to remonstrate, but nobody listened.
What Makes It Different From Similar Words

Protest is its closest everyday cousin. But "protest" can be public, collective, and sometimes emotional (a street protest, for example). Remonstrate is almost always personal and face-to-face — one person addressing another, or a group addressing those responsible — with the emphasis on reasoned appeal.

Complain is weaker and more passive. You can complain to anyone, even someone unrelated to the problem. Remonstrating targets the person who has the power to change things.

Object is cooler and more neutral — simply stating disagreement. Remonstrating is more engaged and more earnest; it carries greater emotional weight and effort.

Argue is broader and doesn't necessarily involve disagreement with a person in authority or someone who has done something questionable. Remonstrating has a built-in sense that something needs to be corrected.

This is a formal word. You will not typically hear someone say in casual conversation, "I remonstrated with my roommate about the dishes." They would more likely say "I had a go at my roommate" or "I confronted them."

Remonstrate appears more often in:

  • Formal writing and literature
  • News reporting (especially historical or political)
  • Academic or legal contexts
  • Any context where the speaker wants to convey measured, dignified objection

So when you do encounter it — in a novel, a newspaper, or a formal document — it signals that someone raised a reasoned, earnest objection in a composed but serious manner.
All the Forms of the Word You Will Encounter

FormWord
Base verbremonstrate
Presentremonstrates
Pastremonstrated
Ongoing actionremonstrating
Noun (the act)remonstrance or remonstration
The person doing itremonstrant

Example of the noun: "Her remonstrance was ignored by the committee."
(Her reasoned, earnest protest was dismissed.)
One Sentence to Lock It In

If you want a single mental anchor for this word, remember this:

To remonstrate is to firmly and earnestly tell someone — to their face and with reasons — that you believe they are wrong or that something must change.

Every time you see this word, that is exactly what is happening.
13594:
A remonstration is a strong, earnest expression of protest or objection — made directly to the person responsible for something you disagree with or find wrong — with the clear intention of making them reconsider or stop.

It is, in other words, the act of pushing back seriously and purposefully against someone's action, decision, or behavior — not in a timid or casual way, but with force and conviction.
What it really means — the core idea

Imagine your colleague keeps interrupting you in meetings. One day, you've had enough. You go to them privately and say, clearly and firmly: "I need you to stop cutting me off. It's disrespectful, and it undermines my work." You're not shouting. You're not gossiping about it with others. You're pressing your case directly — earnestly, seriously — with the goal of changing their behavior.

That act — that direct, firm, purposeful objection made face-to-face with someone — is a remonstration.

A few things are always true of a remonstration:

  • It is directed at someone. You don't remonstrate in a vacuum. A remonstration is aimed at a specific person (or group) — the one doing the thing you object to. You make a remonstration to someone, or with someone.
  • It is earnest and serious. It is not casual grumbling or a passing remark. There is weight and sincerity to it.
  • It carries a purpose. The person making the remonstration wants the other person to stop, reconsider, or change course. It's not just venting — it's a plea backed by reasons or moral conviction.
  • It is verbal or communicative. A remonstration is expressed — spoken, written, or otherwise clearly communicated. It is not a private feeling kept to oneself.

• It is not simply complaining to a third party about someone. That's more of a grievance or a lament.
  • It is not passive or timid. A quiet murmur of mild dissatisfaction is not a remonstration.
  • It is not a punishment or a consequence. You are not penalizing someone — you are appealing to them, even if firmly.
  • It is not necessarily angry. A remonstration can be perfectly calm and composed in tone, yet still firm and forceful in its message.
How it compares to similar words

Protest is the closest common word. A remonstration is a type of protest, but more specific: it is typically personal and direct (aimed at the responsible party), whereas a protest can be public, anonymous, or aimed at no one in particular (like a street protest against a government policy).

Objection is milder and more neutral. An objection is simply a point of disagreement. A remonstration is an objection with more emotional weight, purpose, and earnestness behind it.

Reproach focuses on expressing blame or disappointment after something has already gone wrong. A remonstration, on the other hand, is often trying to prevent or stop something — it's forward-looking, or at least action-seeking.

Rebuke is harsher. A rebuke is about correcting or reprimanding someone, often from a position of authority. A remonstration does not require any authority — anyone can make one to anyone. It is more of a plea with reasons than a telling-off.

Expostulation is the nearest synonym — almost interchangeable. It is just an older, rarer word meaning the same thing.

The plural is remonstrations. It is very common to see it in the plural, often to convey that someone protested multiple times or raised multiple objections:

"Despite her repeated remonstrations, the policy remained unchanged."

This sentence tells you: she pushed back — earnestly, directly, more than once — and it still didn't work.

Remonstration is a formal-to-literary word. You will rarely hear it in everyday casual conversation. People would instead say "complaint," "objection," "pushback," or "protest" in daily speech.

You are most likely to encounter remonstration in:

  • Literature (classic and modern novels)
  • Journalism and formal writing
  • Historical or political texts
  • Legal or official documents

If you were writing a formal letter to a company, a newspaper editorial, or a scene in a novel, remonstration would feel perfectly at home.

Here are several sentences across different tones and contexts, so you can feel the word in action:

  1. "The student's remonstration was calm but clear — she explained to the professor exactly why she believed the grading was unfair."
    → A polite but serious objection made directly to the person responsible.
  2. "No amount of remonstration from the public could convince the committee to reverse its decision."
    → Earnest protests made by many people, aimed at the decision-makers, but without success.
  3. "He made a quiet remonstration to his friend about the unkind remark, and the friend apologized at once."
    → A direct, private, firm-but-not-aggressive objection that achieved its purpose.
  4. "Her remonstrations went unheard for years — until finally, someone in power listened."
    → Repeated, earnest attempts to make someone see the problem and change.
  5. "The letter was a formal remonstration against the new policy, signed by over forty professors."
    → A written, organized, official protest directed at those in charge.

If you ever need to recall what remonstration means, think of it this way:

A remonstration is a serious, earnest, direct pushback — aimed at the right person, with the hope of changing something.

That is the word in full.
13595:
Remorse is a deep, painful feeling of guilt and regret that you get after you have done something wrong — something that hurt another person, broke a moral rule, or violated your own sense of right and wrong. It is not just thinking "I wish I hadn't done that." It goes much deeper than that. It is a feeling that eats at you from inside, a heavy, uncomfortable weight in your heart that won't easily go away.

The key thing about remorse is that it always points backward — to something you already did. You cannot feel remorse about something you haven't done yet.

Remorse is not a quiet or gentle feeling. It is heavy and often painful. When a person feels remorse, they typically experience a mix of things all at once: guilt over what they did, sorrow for the pain they caused, and a strong wish that they could go back in time and undo their action. There is often a sense of self-blame — you look at yourself and think, "I did that. That was wrong. I am responsible."

It can also come with a feeling of shame, though remorse and shame are not the same thing (more on this shortly). The pain of remorse can linger for a long time, sometimes for years, or even a lifetime.

Remorse is triggered by your own actions — things you did, said, or chose. Common causes include:

Hurting someone you love through your words or behavior. Betraying someone's trust. Making a selfish choice that had harmful consequences for others. Lying. Acting violently. Neglecting someone who needed you. Doing something you knew was wrong at the time, or something you only later realized was wrong.

Importantly, remorse requires moral awareness — you have to be able to recognize that what you did was wrong. A person who has no moral compass cannot genuinely feel remorse.

Remorse sits at the strong end of the emotional scale. Think of emotions on a scale from mild to intense:

Mild → Regret → Guilt → Remorse → Deep/Crushing Remorse

It is stronger than simple regret. You can regret ordering the wrong food at a restaurant — that is a minor, almost emotionless disappointment. You cannot really feel "remorse" about that, because nothing morally wrong happened. Remorse requires a moral dimension — a sense that you wronged someone or something.

This is where many learners get confused, so let's separate these carefully.

Remorse vs. Regret: Regret is broader and softer. You can regret missing an opportunity, regret a bad decision that only hurt yourself, or regret something that wasn't even your fault. Remorse is narrower and stronger — it specifically involves feeling bad about a moral wrong that you actively committed. All remorse involves some regret, but not all regret is remorse.

Remorse vs. Guilt: These are very close, and people often use them interchangeably, but there is a subtle difference. Guilt is the feeling of having broken a rule or done something wrong — it is more focused on the act itself. Remorse includes guilt but adds a deeper layer: sorrow for the harm caused to others. Remorse is more empathetic — it is not just "I broke the rule" but "I hurt someone, and I feel genuine pain about that."

Remorse vs. Shame: Shame is about your identity — it makes you feel like you are a bad person. Remorse is about your action — it makes you feel like you did a bad thing. Shame says "I am worthless." Remorse says "What I did was wrong, and I wish I could make it right." This is actually an important distinction — remorse is considered healthier than shame, because it focuses on fixing the behavior rather than collapsing your sense of self.

Remorse vs. Repentance: Repentance is what often follows remorse, especially in a religious or moral context. When you repent, you are actively turning away from the wrong behavior and committing to change. Remorse is the painful feeling; repentance is the response to that feeling.

Genuine remorse is not just passive suffering. It often motivates action. A person truly feeling remorse may:

Apologize sincerely to the person they hurt. Try to make amends or repair the damage they caused. Change their behavior so they don't repeat the same wrong. Seek forgiveness — from the person they hurt, from God (in religious contexts), or from themselves.

This is what separates genuine remorse from performing it. Real remorse compels you toward accountability and change. If someone claims remorse but makes no effort to apologize or change, many people would question whether their remorse is real.

The phrase "without remorse" is very commonly used, and understanding it deepens your understanding of the word itself. When someone does something terrible without remorse, it means they feel no guilt, no sorrow, no pain about what they did. It signals a coldness or cruelty that society finds deeply disturbing. You will often see this phrase in legal, moral, and literary contexts to describe people who cause harm and feel nothing about it — it paints a picture of someone dangerous and morally disconnected.

These are the natural word combinations you will encounter with "remorse":

Feel remorse — the most basic usage. She felt deep remorse after the argument.

Show remorse — to express or demonstrate the feeling outwardly. The judge asked whether the defendant showed any remorse.

Express remorse — similar to "show," but often more verbal or formal. He expressed remorse for his actions during the interview.

Deep/genuine/sincere remorse — these adjectives emphasize that the feeling is real and strong, not fake.

A pang of remorse — a sudden, sharp moment of feeling remorse. A pang of remorse hit him when he saw how much he had hurt her.

Filled with remorse / overwhelmed with remorse — to be completely overtaken by the feeling.

Without remorse — as discussed above, meaning with no guilt or regret.

Here are sentences that show how "remorse" is used naturally:

After shouting at his younger brother, he was filled with remorse and immediately went to apologize.

The criminal showed no remorse during his trial, which shocked everyone in the courtroom.

Years later, she still carried the remorse of having abandoned her friend when she needed her most.

A pang of remorse struck him as he realized how selfish his decision had been.

Her tears and words of remorse convinced the family that she was genuinely sorry.
One Final Thought to Anchor the Word

If you want one simple image to remember "remorse" by, think of it this way:

Remorse is your conscience refusing to let you forget the harm you caused.

It is the voice inside you that says: "You did something wrong. Someone was hurt because of you. You cannot just move on as if nothing happened." It is uncomfortable precisely because it is moral — it is your inner sense of right and wrong doing its job. And when it leads a person to take responsibility and change, remorse becomes one of the most important and humanizing emotions there is.
13596: Remorseful describes how you feel when you have done something wrong — something that hurt another person — and you feel deep, painful guilt and sorrow about it. It is not a small or mild feeling. It is a heavy, aching feeling that tells you from the inside: "What I did was wrong. I wish I had never done it."
Three things are always true when someone is remorseful

1. They did something wrong — something that hurt another person or violated their own moral values.
  2. They know it was wrong — they accept full responsibility, with no excuses.
  3. They feel genuine, lasting pain about it — not a quick "oops," but a deep, lingering sadness.

Imagine you said something very cruel to your closest friend in a moment of anger. The next day, when the anger fades, you realize how badly your words hurt them. You can't stop thinking about it. You feel sick about what you did. You wish you could go back in time and unsay those words. You desperately want to make it right.

That heavy, painful feeling — a mix of guilt, sorrow, and the wish to undo the harm — is remorse. And the word that describes you in that state is remorseful.

• "She was deeply remorseful after lying to her parents."
  • "The man stood in court looking genuinely remorseful for his crime."
  • "He said he was sorry, but he didn't seem remorseful at all."
  • "Years later, she remained remorseful about the way she had treated him."

You'll often see it strengthened with words like deeply, truly, or genuinely — because remorse is naturally an intense emotion, and these words underline its sincerity.
How "remorseful" is different from similar words

This is where most learners get confused. Here are the key differences:

Remorseful vs. Sorry
"Sorry" is casual and broad. You can say "I'm sorry I'm late" without any real emotional weight. Remorseful always carries deep, sincere guilt about a moral wrong. You would never say you're remorseful about being five minutes late — that word is far too serious for minor inconveniences.

Remorseful vs. Regretful
Regretful means you wish something had gone differently — but that "something" can include things outside your control. "I'm regretful that I missed the concert" (the tickets sold out — not your fault). Remorseful is used only when you yourself did something wrong. You cannot be remorseful about bad weather. You can only be remorseful about your own actions.

Remorseful vs. Guilty
Feeling guilty means you recognize you did something wrong. Remorseful goes a step further — it adds deep emotional pain, sorrow, and the aching wish to undo the harm. Someone can feel guilty but push that feeling aside and move on. A person who is remorseful is actively sitting in that heavy moral pain, not running from it.

Remorseful vs. Ashamed
Shame is often about how others see you — it involves fear of judgment and embarrassment in front of people. Remorse is more personal and inward — it's about what your actions did to another person, regardless of whether anyone else knows. A politician might feel ashamed of a scandal (worried about public image) without being at all remorseful (without genuinely caring about who was harmed).

• For trivial mistakes: "I'm remorseful about forgetting to buy milk" — this sounds odd and overdramatic. The word is reserved for genuinely serious wrongs.
  • For things outside your control: "She was remorseful that her father got sick" — wrong usage. You can only be remorseful about your own choices and actions, never about circumstances.
  • For non-moral situations: "I'm remorseful that the weather was bad on vacation" — this is incorrect. Remorse always has a moral dimension.

The adjective "remorseful" comes from the noun remorse — which is the feeling itself:

  • "He was filled with remorse." → noun (the feeling)
  • "He was remorseful." → adjective (describing the person)

Both carry identical emotional weight. The only difference is grammar.
The one thing to always remember

Remorseful is a word about a person's conscience — their inner moral pain. When someone is truly remorseful, they are not just saying sorry to look good or to avoid punishment. They genuinely feel the weight of what they did to another person. That is what separates real remorse from a hollow, surface-level apology — and that is exactly what this word captures.
13597:
To understand remorseless, you first need to understand remorse.

Remorse is that deep, painful feeling of guilt and regret you get after doing something wrong — especially something that hurt another person. It's the feeling that eats at you from inside. It's heavier than ordinary regret. When someone feels remorse, they genuinely wish they hadn't done what they did, and they feel the weight of their wrongdoing emotionally.

Think of a person who lied to a close friend and caused them real harm. If they feel remorse, they lose sleep over it. They feel ashamed. They want to apologize, make things right.

Remorseless, then, means the complete absence of that feeling. No guilt. No regret. No internal pain about the wrong done. Zero.
The two main ways "remorseless" is used

This word is used in two distinct but connected senses. Both are equally correct and common.

Sense 1 — Applied to people or their actions

When you call a person remorseless, you mean they did something harmful, cruel, or wrong — and they feel absolutely no guilt about it whatsoever. They are emotionally cold about it. The suffering they caused does not trouble them. There is no softening, no regret, no conscience gnawing at them.

This is a strong, dark word when used this way. It paints someone as emotionally hardened or morally indifferent — someone who can harm others and simply... not care.

"The judge called him a remorseless criminal who showed no sign of guilt even after the verdict."

"She described her attacker as remorseless — he looked straight at her during the trial without a flicker of regret."

It can also be applied to actions or behavior — meaning the action itself is carried out without any guilt or hesitation:

"The army advanced with remorseless cruelty, destroying everything in its path."

"He pursued his rivals with remorseless aggression, never pausing to question what he was doing to them."

Sense 2 — Applied to forces, processes, or things (the metaphorical use)

Here, the word detaches from guilt entirely. It is used to describe things — not people — that are relentless, unstoppable, and show no signs of pausing or softening. The connection to the original meaning is this: just as a remorseless person never softens or holds back, a remorseless force never lets up or slows down.

This use is extremely common in writing, journalism, and literature.

"The remorseless advance of time waits for no one."

"The desert sun beat down with remorseless intensity."

"They worked under remorseless pressure to meet the deadline."

"Climate change is a remorseless process — it doesn't stop because we find it inconvenient."

Notice how in these sentences, there is no question of guilt or regret. The time, the sun, the pressure obviously cannot feel remorse. The word is being used here to mean: unrelenting, without pause, without mercy, unstoppable.
The tone and feeling this word carries

Remorseless is not a neutral word. It almost always has a dark, serious, or ominous tone. It suggests something heavy — either a person stripped of conscience, or a force that grinds forward without any softness.

When used about people, it often implies that the person is dangerous or deeply unsympathetic. It's the kind of word used in courtrooms, crime reporting, or serious fiction.

When used about forces or processes, it creates a feeling of inevitability — something is coming, and nothing will stop it.
How it differs from similar words

Several words are close to remorseless, but each has a slightly different focus. Understanding these differences sharpens your understanding of all of them.

Ruthless — focused on a willingness to harm others in pursuit of a goal. A ruthless person will do whatever it takes, even if it hurts others. The focus is on the goal and the disregard for others in reaching it.

A ruthless businessman fires hundreds of workers without hesitation to increase profit.

Merciless — focused on the refusal to show mercy to someone who is suffering or begging for relief. A merciless person will not let up even when the other person is clearly in pain or asking to stop.

A merciless interrogator keeps pushing even when the suspect is exhausted and broken.

Pitiless — almost identical to merciless, but slightly more focused on feeling no pity for the suffering of others.

Callous — focused on being emotionally hardened and unaffected by others' pain. A callous person has become so indifferent that they don't even register that someone is suffering.

Unrepentant — focused on not being sorry and not wanting to change. Close to remorseless but slightly different: an unrepentant person knows they did wrong and simply doesn't care to apologize or change. A remorseless person may not even acknowledge the wrong at all — there's no internal emotional response.

Relentless — focused on never stopping or giving up, regardless of obstacles. This is the closest to Sense 2 of remorseless. But relentless is usually more neutral or even positive (a relentless athlete), while remorseless in this sense still carries a heavier, more ominous feel.

The specific thing that makes remorseless unique is its direct reference to the absence of that particular deep guilt called remorse — the emotional reckoning that most people feel after causing harm. When someone is remorseless, that internal alarm simply doesn't go off.

Remorseless is a strong word. It's not something you use lightly or casually. You wouldn't describe someone as remorseless just for being a bit rude or inconsiderate. It's used for serious wrongdoing, cruelty, or powerful unstoppable forces. Reserve it for contexts where the stakes are high.

Core meaningHaving or showing no remorse (no guilt, no regret)
Applied to peopleCold, hardened, feeling no guilt after causing harm
Applied to forces/thingsRelentless, unstoppable, never letting up
ToneDark, serious, ominous
IntensityStrong — not a word for minor situations
A few more example sentences to cement it

"The serial offender was described by prosecutors as remorseless — he had never once expressed any regret for his crimes."

"History judges the colonizers as remorseless in their exploitation of local populations."

"The river rose with remorseless force, swallowing everything on its banks."

"She faced the remorseless grind of poverty that never gave her a moment's relief."

"He watched his opponent with remorseless focus, never blinking, never hesitating."

That's the full picture of remorseless — its meaning, its two uses, its tone, its distinctions from similar words, and how it works in real sentences. You now have everything you need.
13598: The word "remote" has one central idea: distance and separation. Everything else flows from that. But this distance isn't always about physical space — it can describe distance in time, in probability, in emotional warmth, and in connection. Once you feel that core idea, all the meanings of this word fall into place naturally.

This is the most common meaning. A remote place is one that is physically far from people, cities, or civilization — and typically hard to reach. A remote village is not just far away; it is isolated. A remote island has no easy road or transport to it. A remote area of a forest is deep inside, away from trails and human activity.

The key thing that separates "remote" from simply "far" is that sense of isolation. A major city in another country might be far away, but it is not remote — it is busy, well-connected, and easy to get to. Remote places are cut off from the rest of the world in some meaningful way.

You'll see it used like this: a remote location, a remote region, a remote outpost, remote terrain.

"Remote" also describes time that is at a great distance from the present — usually the very distant past, though sometimes the far future.

"In the remote past, this land was covered by a vast sea."
"The remote origins of this tradition are unclear."

This usage appears more in writing and academic contexts than in everyday speech. The feeling it gives is of enormous time — so far back that it feels almost unreachable, much like a faraway place.
Very unlikely — a remote chance or possibility

This is one of the most important and frequently used meanings, and it often trips up learners, so pay close attention.

When something is described as a remote chance or a remote possibility, it means the probability is extremely small — barely worth counting on.

"There's a remote chance the flight will be on time."
"Don't get your hopes up — the possibility is remote."

Think of likelihood as a long line. At one end sits "certain," and at the very far other end sits "remote possibility." The remote possibility is so far from certainty that it barely exists. It's not quite zero — but nearly.

One subtle but important nuance: "remote" here suggests the speaker is consciously acknowledging that a possibility exists, while at the same time gently dismissing it as negligible. It's a very specific shade of "unlikely." More so than "small chance." You'd say a remote chance when you want to suggest: don't count on this.

When a person is described as remote, it means they seem cold, detached, or emotionally unreachable. They may be physically present but feel far away in spirit. They don't engage warmly, they don't share what they're thinking or feeling, and they're difficult to truly connect with.

"He was polite, but remote — the conversation never got past the surface."
"After the loss, she became remote and withdrawn."

Being remote doesn't mean being rude or hostile. It simply means there's an invisible gap between the person and those around them — like a glass wall. You can see them, but you can't quite reach them. This is a metaphorical use of the distance idea: the person's inner self is far away, even when their body is nearby.

"Remote" can also describe a link between two things that is very thin, indirect, or hard to trace clearly.

"There is a remote connection between the two crimes."
"She bears a remote resemblance to her grandmother."

In the first example, the connection exists but is weak — perhaps a shared coincidence, not a clear cause-and-effect. In the second, the resemblance is slight — you might notice it only if you look carefully. The word signals that the link is there, but just barely — at a great distance from being obvious or strong.
Used in modern work and technology

In recent years, "remote" has taken on a very practical meaning in work and technology.

Remote work (or a remote job) means working from a location away from the office — most often from home. You are doing your job from a distance, without being physically present at the workplace.

Remote access refers to connecting to a computer, system, or file from a different location, usually over the internet. You don't need to be physically sitting in front of the machine to use it.

A remote control — which you likely already know — lets you operate a device like a TV or a drone from a distance, without touching it.

In every case here, the idea is the same as always: doing something across a distance, from a separated location.

Every single meaning of "remote" comes back to the same core feeling: something is far away, separated, or hard to reach. Whether it's a desert island cut off from the world, a tiny sliver of probability almost too small to consider, a person who keeps the world at arm's length, or a colleague working from across the country — remote always signals a significant gap, a meaningful distance between something and where it might otherwise be close.

A mental image that ties it all together: picture the very edge of a map — the outermost point, where the land runs out and there is nothing familiar beyond it. That distant, hard-to-reach feeling is what remote carries in every context it appears in.
13599:
To remunerate someone means to pay them for work, a service, or an effort they have performed. It is the act of giving a person money — or sometimes other forms of compensation — as a reward for something they have done for you.

Think of it as a transaction of fairness: you did something for me, so I owe you something in return, and I am now giving it to you.

Simple example:

"The hospital will remunerate the doctors for their overtime work."
(= The hospital will pay the doctors for their extra hours.)
The key idea within the word

What sets "remunerate" apart from just saying "pay" is the strong sense that the payment is earned and deserved — it is not a gift, a charity, or a random gesture. It implies a clear link between what was given (time, skill, effort, a service) and what is being returned (money or its equivalent).

Occasionally, it can also mean compensating someone for a loss or expense they suffered — not just for work done. But in the vast majority of cases, you will encounter it in the context of paying for professional work or services.

Very. Remunerate is a formal word. You would almost never use it in a casual conversation with friends. It belongs to professional and official settings, such as:

  • Employment contracts ("the employee shall be remunerated monthly")
  • Business negotiations
  • Legal and HR documents
  • Economic and policy discussions
  • Formal journalism

In everyday life, people simply say pay. But in formal writing or speech, "remunerate" is chosen to sound precise and professional.

Here are several examples showing how the word is used across different situations:

  1. "The firm agreed to remunerate its consultants at a competitive rate."
    → The firm agreed to pay its consultants well.
  2. "She was generously remunerated for her years of service."
    → She received a generous payment for her years of work.
  3. "The company failed to remunerate its workers for overtime."
    → The company did not pay workers for the extra hours they put in.
  4. "How will the government remunerate the volunteers who risked their lives?"
    → How will the government compensate those volunteers?
  5. "He remunerates his staff fairly, which is why turnover is so low."
    → He pays his staff fairly, which is why very few people leave.
How it compares to similar words

These words are all related to payment, but each one has a different shade of meaning:

Pay is the plain, everyday word with no special connotation. You pay for groceries, rent, and taxi rides. "Remunerate" is reserved specifically for rewarding professional work or formal services.

Compensate is broader. You can compensate someone for a loss (like an accident or an injury), not just for work done. "Remunerate" is more specific — it focuses on work or service provided.

Reimburse means to pay someone back for money they already spent out of their own pocket. If you bought office supplies yourself and your employer refunds that cost to you, that's reimbursement — not remuneration.

Reward can be non-monetary — a trophy, praise, a thank-you note. "Remunerate" almost always involves actual money or formal compensation of measurable value.

Recompense is a formal, somewhat old-fashioned word meaning to make payment for loss, trouble, or damage. It overlaps with both "compensate" and "remunerate," but "remunerate" is the clearest choice when the context is specifically about paying for services rendered.
All the forms of this word

Knowing the related forms helps you recognize and use this word family in any situation:

  • Remunerate — the verb itself ("They will remunerate the team by Friday.")
  • Remunerated — past tense ("The freelancer was remunerated last week.")
  • Remunerating — ongoing action ("The firm is currently remunerating its contractors.")
  • Remuneration — the noun, meaning the payment or compensation itself ("His remuneration includes a base salary, bonus, and health benefits.") — this noun form is actually very common in business writing, perhaps even more so than the verb.
  • Remunerative — the adjective, used to describe something that pays well or is financially rewarding ("Medicine is a demanding but highly remunerative profession.")

People sometimes mix up remunerate with the completely unrelated word enumerate, which means to list or count things one by one (like "Let me enumerate the reasons..."). They look and sound vaguely similar, but they share no meaning at all. If you get confused, just remember: remunerate = repay, enumerate = list.
To remunerate someone = to pay them what they have earned for their work, service, or effort — almost always in a formal, professional context.
